title: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start and a new interval to insert, insert the new interval and merge any overlaps so the result remains a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals. Solve it with the three-phase merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Insert Interval (Insert and Merge into a Sorted Interval List)

s1_definition.profdef: The insert interval problem takes an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and produces the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging the new interval with any it overlaps. Because the input is already sorted, it is solved in a single linear pass in three phases: copy intervals that end before the new one begins, merge all intervals that overlap the new one into an expanded interval, then copy the remaining intervals that start after the merged interval ends.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh already has a tidy, sorted list of distinct account-hold periods and now needs to add one more hold that may overlap some existing ones. He walks the list once: he keeps every hold that finishes before the new hold starts untouched, he fuses the new hold with every hold it bumps into to form one bigger hold, and then he keeps the rest of the holds that begin after the new fused hold ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: In one pass, copy intervals before, merge intervals overlapping the new one, then copy intervals after.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The insert interval problem takes an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and produces the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging the new interval with any it overlaps. Because the input is already sorted, it is solved in a single linear pass in three phases: copy intervals that end before the new one begins, merge all intervals that overlap the new one into an expanded interval, then copy the remaining intervals that start after the merged interval ends.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh already has a tidy, sorted list of distinct account-hold periods and now needs to add one more hold that may overlap some existing ones. He walks the list once: he keeps every hold that finishes before the new hold starts untouched, he fuses the new hold with every hold it bumps into to form one bigger hold, and then he keeps the rest of the holds that begin after the new fused hold ends.

**One line to remember:** In one pass, copy intervals before, merge intervals overlapping the new one, then copy intervals after.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the existing intervals are already sorted by start and are non-overlapping, we do not need to sort again, which lets us solve the problem in a single linear pass rather than n log n. We process the list in three clearly separated phases, which keeps the logic clean and avoids edge-case tangles.

In the first phase we copy, unchanged, every existing interval that ends strictly before the new interval starts, because such an interval lies entirely to the left of the new one and can never overlap it. The condition is `while (i < n && intervals[i].end < newInterval.start) result.add(intervals[i++]);`. In the second phase we merge: every remaining interval whose start is at or before the new interval's end overlaps it, so we fold it into the new interval by setting the new start to the minimum of the two starts and the new end to the maximum of the two ends. We keep doing this with `newStart = Math.min(newStart, intervals[i].start); newEnd = Math.max(newEnd, intervals[i].end); i++;` while the overlap condition holds, and once the loop ends we add the single expanded interval to the result.

In the third phase we copy, unchanged, all remaining intervals, which necessarily start after the merged interval ends and therefore do not overlap it. The senior-level nuance is that the merge phase must take the minimum of the starts as well as the maximum of the ends, because the new interval might begin before some overlapping existing interval, and that it must continue consuming intervals as long as they overlap, since the new interval can swallow several existing ones at once.

We build a fresh result list and do not mutate the input. The time complexity is linear, O(n), a single pass since the input is pre-sorted, and the space complexity is O(n) for the result. This three-phase structure is the standard clean solution and demonstrates that we exploit the pre-sorted precondition rather than redundantly re-sorting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the account-hold system maintains a sorted, non-overlapping list of periods during which an account is on hold, and when a new hold is requested, perhaps for a fresh fraud investigation, it must be inserted into the list and merged with any existing holds it overlaps so the account's hold schedule stays a clean non-overlapping timeline. This is exactly the insert interval problem, and because the existing schedule is already sorted the insertion should be a fast single pass.

Problem 2 — Rebuilding and re-sorting the whole schedule on every new hold is wasteful when the list is already sorted. The three-phase single-pass insertion keeps the operation linear, which matters because holds are added frequently and the schedule can be long.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `Interval` class for a hold period, a `HoldScheduleService` with an `insertHold` method implementing the three phases, and a runnable `InsertIntervalDemo` main class that inserts a new hold into Rajesh's and Priya's sorted schedules, logging each phase at fine level and the resulting schedule at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's sorted schedule is [1,2], [3,5], [6,7], [8,10], [12,16] and the new hold is [4,9]. We build an empty result and start at index 0.

Phase 1, copy holds ending before the new hold starts at 4: the first hold [1,2] ends at 2, which is less than 4, so copy it, move to index 1. The next hold [3,5] ends at 5, which is not less than 4, so phase 1 stops.

Phase 2, merge overlapping holds. The new interval starts as start 4, end 9. The hold [3,5] has start 3 which is at or before the new end 9, so overlap: new start becomes the minimum of 4 and 3 which is 3, new end becomes the maximum of 9 and 5 which is 9. Move to index 2. The hold [6,7] has start 6 at or before 9, overlap: new start stays 3, new end stays the maximum of 9 and 7 which is 9. Move to index 3. The hold [8,10] has start 8 at or before 9, overlap: new start stays 3, new end becomes the maximum of 9 and 10 which is 10. Move to index 4. The hold [12,16] has start 12 which is greater than 10, so phase 2 stops. We add the merged interval [3,10] to the result.

Phase 3, copy remaining holds: [12,16] is copied. Index reaches the end.

The resulting schedule for Rajesh is [1,2], [3,10], [12,16].

2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Phase 2 merge [3,5] → [3,9]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Phase 2 merge [6,7] → [3,9]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Phase 2 merge [8,10] → [3,10]
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Phase 3 keep [12,16]

sections.s6_takeaway:
The insert interval problem gives me an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and asks for the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging. Because the input is already sorted, I solve it in a single linear pass rather than re-sorting, which I do in three clearly separated phases to keep the edge cases tidy. In the first phase I copy every existing interval that ends before the new interval starts, since those lie entirely to the left and cannot overlap. In the second phase I merge every interval whose start is at or before the new interval's end, folding each into the new interval by taking the minimum of the starts and the maximum of the ends. In the third phase I copy the remaining intervals, which all start after the merged interval and cannot overlap.

The details I always emphasize are that the merge phase takes the minimum of the starts, not just the maximum of the ends, because the new interval may begin before some overlapping existing interval, and that the merge continues consuming intervals as long as they overlap, because one new interval can swallow several existing ones at once, exactly as it did when my new hold absorbed three existing holds in the example.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the account-hold system. We maintained a sorted, non-overlapping schedule of periods during which an account was on hold, and whenever a new hold was requested, often for a fresh fraud investigation, we inserted it and merged it with any existing overlapping holds so the schedule stayed a clean non-overlapping timeline. Because the existing schedule was already sorted, the three-phase single pass kept each insertion linear, which mattered since holds were added frequently and schedules could be long.

The senior-level point I make is that this problem rewards exploiting the pre-sorted precondition: a candidate who re-sorts has missed that the whole value is doing it in one linear pass, and the three-phase structure is what makes that pass both correct and readable. I also stress the minimum-of-starts rule and the multi-interval absorption as the two places people slip, and I note that this builds directly on the merge-intervals skeleton, just with the sort already done for us. Recognizing the precondition and articulating the clean phasing is what demonstrates to an interviewer that I understand the problem beyond a memorized solution.
